title: Where Two Words Melt Into One
label: ch:fr-contractions
canDo: I can say to, at, of and from, and I know which four combinations of preposition and article melt into a single word.

payoff.summary: Every noun the book owns is put in somebody's hands and put somewhere. Two prepositions and four articles make eight combinations, four of which melt -- and the rule that decides which is the one du already showed: le and les contract, la and l' do not. The u inside au was an l, which is the same eight-century-old change that made chevaux out of cheval.
payoff.note: de la and des were never missing from the language, only from the food chapter's table: every noun on it happened to be a le-word or a vowel-word. des then closes a second point for free, because it is also the plural of un -- the word English never built.
